title: Israeli Strike in Lebanon Kills 12 People From a Single Family, Including 6 Children
author: Katrine Dige Houmøller
content:

local sheikh gives a final prayer over the body of one of six children killed
in a September 7, 2026 Israeli airstrike on the Farhat family home in Kfar
Remman, in Nabatieh district, southern Lebanon that killed a total of 12
members of the family. September 8, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.

KFAR REMMAN, Lebanon--"They are killing children. That's what they're doing,"
Baker Malak said, pointing to the tiny coffins being carried through the
streets of the town of Kfar Remman in southern Lebanon on Tuesday. He walked
alongside hundreds of mourners in a funeral procession to bury 12 members of a
single family, half of them children, killed in an Israeli airstrike on their
home a day earlier.

Nearby, mourners carried the coffin of 18-year-old paramedic Ali Shahrour,
killed in a separate strike on the town the same day. The procession wound
through streets scarred by months of bombardment as an Israeli drone buzzed
incessantly overhead.

"When Israel sees that the Lebanese government is doing nothing, they will
keep targeting children," said Malak.

Israel bombed the three-story family home of the Farhat family on Monday
morning without warning, reducing the entire building to rubble, and killing
three men, three women, and six children between the ages of two months and 13
years. Two other children, both eight years old, were severely wounded in the
strike.

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff3601798-c74d-4d1b-ac97-d227dc1920da_6089x4059.jpeg)The
Farhat family home in Kfar Remman, in Nabatieh district, southern Lebanon
after a September 7, 2026 Israeli airstrike killed 12 members of the family.

Malak, 45, a resident of Kfar Remman, was a close friend of two brothers
killed in the attack, Hassan and Hussein Farhat. Both their coffins were
draped in Hezbollah flags during the funeral. Malak told Drop Site he had seen
the two men 10 days before the strike. He said they were preparing their
children for school after months of closures due to Israel's bombardment. In
the ruins of the family home, schoolbooks, timetables and notebooks lay
scattered among the ruins. The Israeli military claimed without evidence that
it struck Hezbollah operatives transporting weapons in the area. Malak told
Drop Site the house was a civilian home and contained no weapons. Lebanon's
Health Ministry called it a "grave violation of international law."

During the burial procession, a man's voice rang out over a loudspeaker:
"Stand up and say goodbye to our angels"--referring to the six children among
the dead. One of the few survivors, eight-year-old Mustafa Farhat, lost his
entire immediate family in the attack--his parents, siblings and grandparents.
Badly wounded, he remained at Al-Najda Hospital in Nabatieh.

The deadly attack on the Farhat home came as part of an escalated wave of
Israeli strikes across southern Lebanon that killed at least 27 people, and
wounded 69 over the previous three days,
[according](https://www.moph.gov.lb/en/Media/view/84385/13/updated-total-toll-
of-the-aggression-2727-martyrs-
and-8438-wounded#/en/Media/view/86863/27-martyrs-and-69-wounded-in-three-days-
of-attacks) to the Health Ministry. The renewed Israeli assault forced some
20,000 people to flee Nabatieh district last week alone,
[according](https://transcripts.un.org/en/briefing/sg/2026-09-08) to the
United Nations.

The attacks come despite a ceasefire and U.S.-brokered framework agreement
signed in Washington by the governments of Israel and Lebanon on June 26. The
deal requires the Lebanese Armed Forces to disarm Hezbollah before Israel
withdraws from parts of the swathe of Lebanese territory it occupies.
Hezbollah has rejected the deal, which has been criticized for extracting few
guarantees from Israel and placing nearly all obligations on the Lebanese
government. An eighth round of talks between Lebanon and Israel overseen by
Washington is expected later this month.

The talks have proceeded despite nearly daily attacks by Israel on Lebanon.
Between Thursday and Monday, the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, UNIFIL,
[recorded](https://transcripts.un.org/en/briefing/sg/2026-09-08) no less than
528 projectiles fired by the Israeli military. On Sunday alone, it recorded 62
Israeli violations of Lebanese airspace--among the highest daily totals since
June. UNIFIL also detected Israeli airstrikes inside its area of operations
and north of the Litani River. And for the first time since June 21, it also
detected a Hezbollah projectile on Sunday, with the group beginning to
reengage in retaliatory attacks.

Asked on Tuesday whether the escalation was being driven by one side, UN
spokesperson Stephane Dujarric pointed to UNIFIL's observations and said:
"Everyone can draw their own conclusions pretty clearly."

Malak said the continuing strikes have only deepened the conviction among many
in the south that the framework agreement has failed to protect civilians.
"The resistance is the only solution," he said, referring to Hezbollah. He
stressed that people in Nabatieh opposed the Israeli occupation of Lebanese
territory in a variety of ways: with weapons, words, or by refusing to leave
their land.

Malak remained in heavily bombarded Kfar Remman throughout the war,
distributing aid and food, and helping to bury the dead. "I will never leave
my village," he said. "If I ever have to leave, it will be to the grave."

Since the latest phase of the war began in Lebanon on March 2, nearly 4,400
people have been killed, including more than 250 children, and over 12,400
wounded, according to the Health Ministry. Israel has also targeted health
care workers and medical facilities, killing at least 135 emergency workers
and attacking 17 hospitals. On Sunday, an Israeli airstrike completely
destroyed Ghandour Hospital in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, according to the ministry,
which condemned the attack as another violation of the special protections
afforded to medical facilities.

At the funeral in Kfar Remman on Tuesday, Karim Saleh, a 32-year-old paramedic
with Al-Rissala Scouts-- a Lebanese youth and civil defense organization--
stood beside the grave of his friend and colleague, 18-year-old paramedic Ali
Shahrour who was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his car in Kfar Remman at 1
a.m. on Monday.

Saleh, Shahrour, and two other paramedics, Hadi Farhat and Hassan Hamze, had
just finished work at a small restaurant they had recently opened together and
Shahrour was driving them all home. Saleh was dropped off first, but shortly
after he entered his home, he heard the screech of a missile tearing through
the air followed by an explosion. Saleh put on his scouts vest and raced to
the scene. Shahrour, Farhat, and Hamze had been struck in the car. People
managed to pull out Farhat and Hamze from the burning vehicle just before it
exploded. Farhat and Hamze were wounded, but Shahrour was killed.

"Every time I close my eyes I see their faces from that moment. That's why I'm
trying to stay awake, so I don't close my eyes," Saleh told Drop Site, his
yellow emergency worker vest stained with blood and his eyes red from tears
and exhaustion.

When Saleh visited Farhat in the intensive care unit in Al-Najda Hospital,
Farhat's first question was "Where is Ali?" He had only just been taken off
the breathing tube so that he could speak. Saleh said his friend was in shock,
struggling with traumatic memories of the attack. Farhat insisted on attending
his friend Shahrour's funeral Tuesday, but doctors said his condition was too
serious to leave the hospital.

"I'm not going to wash their blood off this vest," Saleh said. "It makes me
feel like I'll always have them by my side."

Shahrour's father, Daniel Sharhour, stood beside him. "They killed him in his
own hometown. In his own car. In his own country," Daniel Sharhour said. As he
spoke, his voice grew louder, drawing people around him. "I will never forgive
what happened to my son. Revenge is hanging around my neck like a necklace. I
will take my revenge. I'm not afraid."
